Here and all other exercises, whenever you encounter `---` in the code chunks, your task is to replace `---` correctly with a variable name, argument, function, code, etc. The instructions will help you. You will not be able to `knit` this RMarkdown document until you completed all tasks.

Load `tidyverse` package (which includes `ggplot2` and many other useful functions for data processing). If you haven't installed `tidyverse`, un-comment (delete the "#") and run the next line:

```{r}
# install.packages("tidyverse")
```

Then, load `tidyverse` using the `library` function.

```{r}
# Load tidyverse
library(tidyverse)
```

We also need the `psyntur` package. Again, if `psyntur` is not installed, please run the `install.packages` command.

```{r}
# install.packages("psyntur")
# Load psyntur
library(psyntur)
```


We are ready to load some data. These data are published in @blomkvist2017reference. Watch out though, the path to the data in the following code depends on the location you saved this RMarkdown in. I'm assuming that 

- you are working in an R Project related to this module,
- that contains (1) a "data" directory with the "blomkvist.csv" data,
- and (2) a directory for "exercises" with another subdirectory for each weeks' exercises (e.g. "week_2").

An organised working environment is important. You can thank me later :)

If the following code return "`Error: '../data/blomkvist.csv' does not exist in current working directory`" you need to check these three steps above.

```{r}
# Load the data
d_blomkvist <- read_csv("../../data/blomkvist.csv")
```


Explore the data `d_blomkvist` with `glimpse`. For now just get an idea of the variables includes in the data and their types (i.e. numeric, categorical).

```{r}
glimpse(---) # replace "---" with the name of the data variable
```

These are average reaction time data for people playing a video game published in @blomkvist2017reference.

Make sure you have an idea of the variable names in the data. For example, `rt_hand_d` means reaction time of hand dominant (`_nd` is for non-dominant, etc.).

Let's start with a scatterplot: `psyntur` has plotting functions that are built around `ggplot2` and allow quick plotting. For example try running this line:

```{r scatterplot, fig.cap="Scatterplot"}
scatterplot(data = d_blomkvist, x = rt_hand_d, y = rt_hand_nd)
```

What does the plot show you? (complete the following sentence)

The scatterplot in Figure \@ref(fig:scatterplot) illustrates ...

Now, the `psyntur` functions are helpful for quick plotting. We are going to focus on `ggplot2` for plotting as it allows for more flexibile and more advanced data visualisation.

Complete the code for the `ggplot2` scatterplot below so it illustrates the same information as the `psyntur` scatterplot, i.e. map the rt of the dominant hand on the x-axis and rt of the non-dominant hand on the y-axis.

```{r}
ggplot(data = d_blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = ---, y = ---)) +
  geom_point()
```

Also, use `Figure \@ref(fig:---)` to crossreference the new `ggplot2` scatterplot in this text.


There are some participants with more extreme values. Let's see who those individuals are. 

Do the following using the code below

1. Map rt of dominant hand on the x-axis and rt of non-dominant hand on the y-axis (as before).
2. Map id on label.
3. Replace `geom_point()` with `geom_text()` or `geom_label()`.

```{r}
ggplot(data = d_blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = ---, y = ---, label = ---)) +
  geom_point()
```

It's hard to see the participants on the lower end. Use the logarithm for both axis to increase the distance between values on the lower end of the scale.

1. `x` and `y` as previously.
2. I've already added `scale_y_log10()` to log transform the y-axis.
3. Do the same for the x-axis.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = ---, y = ---)) +
  geom_point() + # Replace the points with text or labels (see above).
  scale_y_log10() +
  --- # add code to log transform the x axis 
```
